prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks based on magic-wavelength trapping, and their development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I ranked B015 first in my opening ballot, but after reading the eight ballots I move B001 to the top of my preferred configuration. The case rests on the criteria I take most seriously. Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is an original idea, an invention that was then realised in a first strontium lattice clock, so it is not a later or more elegant version of something already done. It has been reproduced in many independent laboratories, which meets my requirement of experimental verification. It also opens a door, in the sense I care about: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, searches for varying constants and dark matter, and the coming redefinition of the second are measurements that could not be made before. Ye's group brought the clock to the 10^-18 regime and established the many-body and systematic-control physics that made that precision believable. Both names are clearly credited, so the committee can be absolutely sure of who did the original work. Four first places and six top-three rankings from seven ranking members also show that this is the one candidate on which the committee is not split by subfield. A two-person prize is clean and leaves room for a different year to take up the other candidates.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is the one Danielsson and Lindroth both raised: after the 2005 prize for the frequency comb and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems and ion clocks, the committee may see the lattice clock as a metrological refinement of an area that has been honoured twice, rather than a new discovery. A related worry is that the headline 10^-18 result is a matter of systematic uncertainty, which is closer to a record than to a discovery. Other groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell) also made decisive steps, and the two-name credit cannot cover them. If the committee holds that the prize is for the original experiment, the case depends on whether the magic-wavelength proposal and first lattice clock are the invention, rather than the later record accuracy. I also give B015 real weight: its original room-temperature observations by Miyazaki and Moodera in 1995 are exactly the kind of original experiment the mandate describes, with large verified benefit in read heads and MRAM. Its weakness is that it has little opening support and the MgO step involves people outside the credited names.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B001 first as a measurement-driven result that nature can check, built on Katori's proposal and driven to 10^-18 by Ye, and he flags whether it is a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the attribution, and I share the refinement worry, though I think it can be answered. The comb prize covered the measurement of optical frequencies and the 2012 prize covered single trapped ions. Neither covered the simultaneous interrogation of many neutral atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength, which removes Doppler and recoil shifts and changes the statistical power of a clock. The citation should therefore be tied to the lattice concept and its realisation, not to precision alone. Where I would push him is on his comparison of B045: I agree the afterglow work has a clear before and after, but the credit gap he notes (van Paradijs, Piro) is a bigger attribution problem than anything in B001, so I would not move it ahead.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B010 first and also puts B015 third, valuing the theory-experiment link in MgO-barrier TMR and noting that the 1995 discovery and the MgO step may belong to different people.
responses.response: We are close on B015 and I thank him for stating the credit split so plainly, since I have the same doubt. I cannot see a three-name prize that is fair to both steps: Miyazaki and Moodera are the original 1995 experiments, while Parkin's MgO work, the Yuasa and Djayaprawira measurements and the Butler and Mathon theory belong to the second step. That is why I keep B015 as an alternative rather than my lead; the committee would have to decide whether it rewards the discovery or the enhancement, and I would not want to credit Parkin on the 1995 discovery. On B010 I respectfully disagree with ranking it first: he himself says that credit among Kane-Mele, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang, Fu-Kane-Mele and Hasan is genuinely split, and a three-person cap forces a cut that I do not think we can defend as the original work today.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B006 (two-dimensional melting and the hexatic phase) first as a simple, general mechanism, and ranks B017 last of his list as probably premature because the superconducting mechanism is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree with him that B017 is open on the pairing mechanism, and I gave it third only because the new platform is a clear case of a tool that lets us see and control phenomena that were inaccessible. On B006 I have to disagree with the ranking. It is an important theory, but the Nobel mandate I work from requires experimental verification, and he says himself that the hexatic evidence is system-dependent and that some melting transitions are first order. Credit also overlaps with Kosterlitz and Thouless, honoured in 2016. I would want the experimental record to settle before the committee commits to a theory prize here.

responses.point: Johansson ranks B003 (circuit QED) first as a new, controllable regime of light-matter interaction with clean, widely reproduced experiments, while noting the proximity to the 2025 prize and that he has programme ties in this area.
responses.response: I take his scientific case seriously and my own opening ranking had B003 sixth. My hesitation is timing and attribution: a second superconducting-circuit prize one year after 2025 will look repetitive to many outside the committee, and the choice among Blais, Girvin, Wallraff and Schoelkopf is unresolved, since I proposed Girvin while Danielsson, Johansson and Lindroth leave him out. I appreciate that he flagged his own ties, and I think he should consider that when we vote on B003. Because he also ranks B001 fifth and says he is outside the area, I would ask him whether he has a specific objection to the Katori and Ye pairing that I am missing.

uncertainties: Whether the committee considers the lattice clock a new discovery or invention, distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or a refinement of the same line.
Whether the committee wants the redefinition of the SI second to be further advanced before honouring the clock.

The relative weight of Ye's group versus other lattice-clock groups (Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell) for priority on the 10^-18 result; I have not independently verified the priority record.
For B015, whether a prize should reward the 1995 discovery or the MgO step, and how to treat Julliere's 1975 low-temperature precursor and the Yuasa group.
Whether B017 is mature enough, given the unresolved pairing mechanism, and how to allocate experimental credit beyond Jarillo-Herrero (Cao, Dean, Efetov, Young).
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B001, B015, B017, B003 or the other shortlisted candidates. None of the credited names appears among my listed co-authors or mentors. I note only that my Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson has flagged programme ties in superconducting circuits (B003), which concerns his own participation and not mine.
